reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Premature ejaculation is the most common male sexual complaint and is defined by ejaculation occurring sooner than desired, with a perceived inability to delay it and associated distress
It is classified as lifelong (present since first sexual experiences) or acquired (developing later after a period of normal control), which guides evaluation and management
Diagnosis is clinical and rests on the history; the intravaginal ejaculatory latency time and degree of control, distress, and interpersonal difficulty frame the assessment
Acquired cases warrant a search for contributing conditions such as erectile dysfunction, thyroid dysfunction, prostatitis, or psychological stressors
Erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation frequently coexist, and treating the erectile problem first may resolve the ejaculatory complaint
Behavioural techniques such as the stop-start and squeeze methods can improve ejaculatory control, often combined with partner involvement and counselling
Pharmacological options work by delaying the ejaculatory reflex, and topical desensitising agents or centrally acting serotonergic medication are used according to principle rather than fixed dosing
A collaborative, non-judgemental approach that addresses relationship and psychological factors improves outcomes
reference.pathophysiology: Ejaculation is a spinal reflex coordinated by sympathetic, parasympathetic, and somatic pathways and modulated by supraspinal serotonergic centres. Serotonin (5-HT) generally raises the ejaculatory threshold, and variation in central serotonergic tone and receptor sensitivity is thought to underlie lifelong premature ejaculation, giving it a substantial neurobiological and genetic basis. Acquired premature ejaculation is more often secondary, arising from erectile dysfunction (where a man rushes before losing his erection), prostatic or thyroid disease, or psychological factors such as anxiety and performance pressure that heighten sympathetic arousal and shorten latency.
additionalDifferentials: Erectile dysfunction with compensatory rapid ejaculation
Chronic prostatitis or pelvic pain contributing to ejaculatory symptoms
Performance anxiety and situational sexual dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Focused sexual and psychosocial history distinguishing lifelong from acquired patterns
Assessment of erectile function to identify coexisting erectile dysfunction
Thyroid function testing when an endocrine cause is suspected
Evaluation for prostatitis or lower urinary tract symptoms where indicated
Screening for depression, anxiety, and relationship stressors
redFlags: Sudden acquired premature ejaculation with erectile dysfunction, which may signal underlying vascular or endocrine disease
Associated pelvic or perineal pain suggesting prostatitis
Significant psychological distress, relationship breakdown, or depression
Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis accompanying new-onset ejaculatory change
reference.prognosis: Premature ejaculation responds well to a combination of behavioural therapy, pharmacological delay of the reflex, and treatment of any coexisting condition, though lifelong forms may require ongoing management to maintain control.
pitfalls: Treating premature ejaculation in isolation while missing coexisting erectile dysfunction
Neglecting the partner and relationship dimension, which strongly influences distress and outcome
Overlooking treatable contributors such as thyroid disease or prostatitis in acquired cases
Framing the problem as purely psychological when a neurobiological basis is likely in lifelong disease
